source_title: Papa John's blames Papa John for big sales decline
company_context: Papa John's International, a publicly traded pizza franchise. Founder/spokesman/chairman John Schnatter caused successive brand crises: November 2017 comments blaming NFL anthem protests for soft sales (he stepped down as CEO in January 2018), then a May 2018 conference call in which he used a racial slur, reported by Forbes in July 2018. He resigned as board chairman on July 11, 2018. Same-store sales fell sharply, but the company survived and restructured.
business_type: Quick-service pizza franchise (publicly listed; franchisor + company stores)
geography: United States (global franchise footprint; HQ Louisville, KY)
macro_context: Competitive QSR/pizza market; brand strongly personified by its founder, who was also the face of advertising, amplifying reputational risk.
outcome_category: 16 - founder/key-person/team failure (founder reputational damage), resolving toward 3 - severe distress but survival
evidence_summary: Founder John Schnatter's public conduct damaged the brand he personified. After November 2017 NFL-protest remarks he stepped down as CEO in January 2018; after a May 2018 conference-call racial slur was reported in July 2018, he resigned as chairman on July 11, 2018. Domestic same-store sales fell sharply in the aftermath (e.g., an 8.1% decline in North America comparable sales in Q4 2018). The Schnatter controversy was reported to have cost the chain about $50.7 million in 2018, with the company and franchisees closing more than 100 locations. The company removed Schnatter from marketing, distanced the brand from him, brought in new leadership/investment, and survived.

source_backed_metrics.ceo_step_down: stepped down as CEO January 2018 (after Nov 2017 NFL remarks)
source_backed_metrics.stock_drop_on_chairman_news: shares fell ~5% (from ~$51.04 to ~$48.42) the day of the chairman resignation
source_backed_metrics.q4_2018_na_comp_sales: North America same-store sales down 8.1% in Q4 2018

owner_decision_context: The board confronted a founder who was simultaneously the brand's marketing face and the source of repeated reputational shocks; it had to sever the brand from the key person to stop revenue bleeding while managing his large ownership stake.
action_taken: Removed Schnatter as CEO then chairman, pulled his image from marketing and stores, pursued a turnaround plan, and brought in new leadership and outside investment (later including a strategic investment by Starboard Value).
outcome_evidence: Severe but survivable: sharp comparable-sales declines (8.1% in Q4 2018), ~$50.7M cost in 2018, 100+ store closures, but the company stabilized and continued operating.
source_limitations: Secondary journalism for the sales/cost figures; the resignation as chairman is also documented in a Papa John's SEC Form 8-K (sec.gov), which could not be fetched here (403). Comparable-sales and cost figures are from reporting on earnings, not quoted verbatim from the 10-K in this record.
directly_stated: Schnatter stepped down as CEO in January 2018 and resigned as chairman July 11, 2018
shares fell ~5% on the chairman-resignation news
North America same-store sales fell 8.1% in Q4 2018
the controversy cost the chain about $50.7 million in 2018
Schnatter owned roughly 30% of the company
inferred: Because the founder personified the brand, his conduct translated directly into demand/sales damage (key-person risk)
Severing brand identity from the key person was the core remedy enabling survival
why_useful_for_opsiq: Clean key-person-risk case where a founder's reputation, fused to brand and demand, produced measurable revenue and store-count damage, then recovered via governed separation from the key person and a turnaround plan. Strong adaptive-trigger example (shock event + demand impact + owner non-compliance with brand norms) with quantified outcomes.
